title: The quail and the hawk
hook: a quail safe in its own field is caught when it strays (SN 47.6)

segments.voice: Yesterday: six animals, and your line, the post holds. When something dragged your attention away, did you feel your feet first? Day three hundred ninety-three.

A hawk drops out of the sky and comes up with a quail in its claws. And the quail, being carried off, starts talking. Not begging. Scolding itself. This is my own fault, it says. I wandered out of my own range into somebody else's. If I'd stayed in my home ground, the ground my mother and father knew, this hawk would be no match for me. The hawk, apparently amused, asks: and where is this home ground of yours? A plowed field, says the quail, covered with clods of earth. Today: the quail and the hawk.
screen: `A QUAIL IN THE HAWK'S CLAWS.` → `I LEFT MY OWN GROUND.` → `A PLOWED FIELD, FULL OF CLODS.`

segments.voice: This is SN 47.6, in the Connected Discourses on mindfulness. The hawk, proud of its strength, lets the quail go. Fine, it says. Go home. Even there you won't escape me. The quail flies back to its plowed field, climbs onto a big clod of earth, and calls up: come and get me now, hawk. The hawk folds its wings and dives at full speed. The quail watches it come, and at the last moment slips down behind the clod. The hawk hits the earth breast first. Then the Buddha explains. Don't wander outside your own range, monks, into the range of others. In others' ground, Mara, the tempter, gets his chance. What isn't your range? The five cords of sense pleasure: sights, sounds, smells, tastes and touches that pull at desire. And what is your own range, the ground your fathers knew? The four foundations of mindfulness: the body, feelings, the mind, and the patterns of experience. Two things stand out. First, the quail isn't stronger than the hawk. It simply knows its ground: every furrow, every clod. Safety in this story isn't power. It's familiarity. Second, the word the text uses for range is gocara, the word for a pasture, the ground a grazing animal knows by heart. Mindfulness, in this picture, isn't a fortress you build. It's a field you know so well you can disappear into it. And the hawk doesn't stop being a hawk. The quail still lives in a world with hawks in it. What changes is where it's standing when one comes.
screen: `THE HAWK LETS THE QUAIL GO.` · `A CLOD IN A PLOWED FIELD.` · `YOUR RANGE: THE FOUR FOUNDATIONS.` · `GOCARA — A PASTURE KNOWN BY HEART.` · then, large: `YOUR OWN GROUND.`

segments.voice: For this sit, your field is small: the breath and the body sitting. Get to know its clods. Where does the breath touch first, at the nostrils or in the chest? Where is the body heavy? When a thought flies off toward someone else's field, a plan, a worry, a screen, notice the moment you've left. Then come back to a clod you know: one breath, one point of contact. Nothing to fight. Just home ground. The bell holds the time.
Gocara, range or pasture. Safety isn't strength; it's staying in your own range, the four foundations of mindfulness.
Your line: your own ground. Today, when you feel yourself drifting somewhere you didn't mean to go, name one thing right in front of you, and stand there. Day three hundred ninety-three.

screen: `DAY 393 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE MONKEY AND THE PITCH.`

howItsDone: In many Buddhist communities, mindfulness is described as a practitioner's own ground or home base, returned to through the day; monastics often keep simple routines and guard the senses when they go into town as a way of staying in that range.

match.prompt: who did what, and what it stands for.

myth: the quail wins because it is stronger than the hawk
it wins because it knows its ground and slips behind a clod.
in this sutta, your own range means the four foundations of mindfulness
body, feelings, mind and the patterns of experience: the ground your fathers knew.
the hawk gives up hunting at the end
the story never says so; the quail just stands where the hawk can't reach it.

fork.setup: you're a quail, caught by a hawk. the hawk lets you go home, sure it can catch you anyway. what do you do?
options: fly as far away as you can
go to your plowed field, stand on a clod, and wait
beg the hawk to leave you alone
fork.reveal: the quail stands on a clod in its own field and calls the hawk down. at the last moment it slips behind the clod, and the hawk hits the earth.

original.note: Pali gocara: range, pasture, the ground a grazing animal knows; the sutta's word for your own range.

trapdoor: what you thought: a fable about a lucky bird.
what it means: stay in your own range, the four foundations of mindfulness, and the hawk can't reach you.
what a scholar hears: gocara, a grazing ground, became a word for a monk's proper range; the quail calls its field its own ancestral domain, sake pettike visaye.

sources.ref: Majjhima Nikaya 10, Satipatthana Sutta (the four foundations)

notes: Story details of SN 47.6 (the quail's lament, the plowed field with clods, the hawk shattering its breast) retold from memory; please confirm.
The phrase 'sake pettike visaye' (own ancestral domain) in the trapdoor: please confirm.
Gocara literally relates to cattle grazing ('where cows go'); the script says 'pasture' to stay safe.
